title: One refused while everyone else bowed.
subtitle: Iblis standing alone in the crowd
then: Right after all the angels bow, one figure stays standing. Ibn Kathir says Iblis, amidst all the angels, {trap}refused out of envy, disbelief, stubbornness, arrogance and false pride{/trap}. The listeners in Makkah were refusing too, after years of hearing the message.
now: The whole family agrees to make peace with your uncle at Eid. Everyone hugs him. You stay in the kitchen. You tell yourself it is principle. {trap}Sometimes standing alone is just pride with a good excuse.{/trap}
old: If I am the only one refusing, I must be the one seeing clearly.
new: Refusing what Allah asks, alone, can be the loneliest form of pride.
try: Think of one place you are refusing to bend, and ask yourself honestly if pride is in it.

title: Allah asked him why, and gave him room to answer.
subtitle: The question before the verdict
then: Before any verdict, Allah asks: {idea}O Iblis, what is the matter with you{/idea} that you are not with those who prostrate? The question gives space. What Iblis does with it shows what is inside him.
now: Your conscience asks you after the argument: why did you say that? You can admit it, or you can build a defense. {idea}The question is a mercy.{/idea} {trap}The defense is where people get stuck.{/trap}
old: When I am questioned, I need to defend myself.
new: Being asked why is a chance to turn back, not a trap to escape.
try: Tonight, ask yourself one honest why about something you did today, and answer without excuses.

title: He looked at the mud and missed the spirit.
subtitle: The first argument from origin
then: Iblis answers with the human's material. Ibn Kathir links it to 7:12, where he says {trap}I am better than him; You created me from fire and him from clay{/trap}, and to 17:62, do you see this one You honored above me. He judged by the stuff, and ignored that Allah had breathed the spirit in.
now: Someone at work did not go to the right university. A relative married into a family you think is beneath yours. {trap}You look at where they came from{/trap} and stop listening. {idea}That was the first sin's logic.{/idea}
old: Where someone comes from tells me what they are worth.
new: Judging people by their origin is the oldest argument, and it was Iblis who made it.
try: Notice one time today you size someone up by background, and drop the thought.

title: Pride took him from the highest place to outside.
subtitle: Get out, you are expelled
then: Ibn Kathir says Allah gave {trap}an unconditional command to Iblis to leave the position he held among the highest of heights{/trap}. He was declared an outcast. The thing he refused to bow to protect, his rank, was exactly what he lost.
now: The manager who would not admit the mistake, to save face, and lost the team's respect anyway. The parent who would not apologize, and lost the child's trust. {trap}Pride guards a position and then costs you that position.{/trap}
old: Admitting I am wrong will make me smaller.
new: Pride promises to protect my standing and is usually what takes it away.
try: Say sorry today for one small thing you would normally let slide.

title: The curse follows him until the Day of Recompense.
subtitle: A refusal that does not stay in the past
then: Ibn Kathir says Iblis was told he {trap}would be followed by a curse that would hound him until the Day of Resurrection{/trap}. One refusal, never repented, became a lasting state. He never asks forgiveness in this scene.
now: A grudge you kept from school. A habit you never quit, first one cigarette, then years. {trap}What you refuse to undo keeps walking with you.{/trap} {idea}The difference for you is that the door to repent is open.{/idea}
old: That thing I did was long ago, it does not matter now.
new: An unrepented wrong does not stay in the past; it follows, unless I turn back.
try: Pick one old wrong you never asked forgiveness for, and ask Allah for it tonight.

title: He asked for more time, not for forgiveness.
subtitle: What Iblis requested once he was expelled
then: Expelled and cursed, Iblis speaks again. He says {trap}My Lord, reprieve me until the Day they are resurrected{/trap}. He calls Allah his Lord, he knows who he is speaking to, and still he asks for time, not mercy.
now: You know the habit is wrong. You do not ask Allah to free you from it. You ask for a bit more time with it. {trap}Just one more year, then I will stop.{/trap} {idea}Ask for the better thing.{/idea}
old: I will deal with it later; I just need a little more time.
new: Asking for time to keep doing wrong is the opposite of asking to be forgiven.
try: Replace one I will stop later with a short dua today asking Allah to help you stop now.

title: Granted time is not the same as approval.
subtitle: Why Iblis was given a reprieve
then: Allah grants it: {trap}you are of those reprieved{/trap}. Ibn Kathir calls it a reprieve until the Day of Resurrection. The curse from two verses before still stands. Iblis gets time, not approval.
now: You did something wrong last month and nothing bad happened. No one found out. Life went on. {trap}It is easy to read that as permission.{/trap} {idea}A delay is not a verdict.{/idea}
old: If nothing bad happened, it must not have been that wrong.
new: Being given time is a test, not a sign that Allah is pleased.
try: Think of one thing you got away with, and set it right quietly today if you can.

title: Even the reprieve has a fixed end date.
subtitle: The Day of the time well-known
then: Iblis asked until the resurrection. Allah answers {idea}until the Day of the time well-known{/idea}. The date is set by Allah, not by Iblis. For a Prophet ﷺ tired of mockery in Makkah, this said: the opposition has an end.
now: You keep slipping on the same thing, over and over. Or someone keeps hurting you and it feels endless. {idea}Every whisper and every harm runs on a clock Allah set.{/idea} It does not get the last word.
new: Even Iblis has a deadline; the pull toward wrong runs out on a day Allah has fixed.
try: When the familiar urge comes today, remind yourself: this has an end, and say a'udhu billah.

title: His method is to make wrong look beautiful.
subtitle: The plan Iblis announced for the earth

row.title: decorated
sub: it looks good, that is the trick

then: Iblis blames Allah for his own error, then reveals his plan. Ibn Kathir explains: {trap}I will make sin dear to them, and encourage, provoke and harass them to commit it{/trap}. His weapon is decoration, not force.
now: The ad never says this will hurt you. The flirt never says this will wreck your marriage. The gossip never says this is backbiting. {trap}It always arrives looking fun, deserved, or harmless.{/trap}
old: I would recognize something wrong because it would feel wrong.
new: Wrong usually arrives decorated; the attractiveness itself is part of the trap.
try: Next time something tempting looks extra appealing, pause and ask what is under the decoration.

title: Even Iblis admitted he cannot reach the sincere.
subtitle: The exception he named himself
then: In the same breath as his threat, Iblis names his own limit: {reward}except Your chosen, sincere servants among them{/reward}. Ibn Kathir compares it to 17:62, where he says he will seize the offspring of Adam all but a few.
now: You worry that you are too weak, too distracted, too tempted. But the line Iblis drew was not strength. It was sincerity. {reward}Doing things for Allah, not for the likes.{/reward} {idea}That is the shield.{/idea}
old: I am too weak to resist the whispers.
new: The protection is sincerity toward Allah, and even Iblis knows he cannot get past it.
try: Do one good deed today that nobody will ever see or know about.

title: Every path ends in front of Allah.
subtitle: The straight way back to Him
then: Allah answers the threat. Ibn Kathir explains it as {idea}all of you will return to Me, and I will reward or punish you according to your deeds{/idea}. He compares it to 89:14, your Lord is ever watchful, and 16:9.
now: You feel like the world is run by whoever shouts loudest or tempts best. The influencer, the scammer, the bully. {idea}Every road, theirs and yours, ends at the same door.{/idea} Walk yours knowing that.
old: The people pulling me off track are winning.
new: Every path leads back to Allah, and He is watching the whole road.
try: Before one decision today, ask: would I be comfortable showing this to Allah?

title: He has no power over you unless you follow.
subtitle: The limit on Iblis, stated by Allah
then: Ibn Kathir narrates that a prophet once asked Iblis how he overpowers people, and Iblis said {trap}I seize him at times of anger and times of desire{/trap}. The prophet answered with 7:200: {idea}seek refuge with Allah{/idea}. Iblis admitted that is how one is saved from him.
now: You are furious in traffic, or scrolling late at night alone. Those are the two openings he named. {trap}Anger and desire.{/trap} {idea}At both moments, a'udhu billah is a real door closing.{/idea}
old: The devil made me do it.
new: Iblis has no authority over me; he only gets in when I follow, mostly through anger or desire.
try: The next time you feel anger or a strong urge, say a'udhu billahi min ash-shaytan ir-rajim.

title: The follower ends up where the leader goes.
subtitle: The promised place of those who follow Iblis
then: Ibn Kathir says {trap}Hell is the abode designated for all those who follow Iblis{/trap}, citing 11:17. The warning comes inside a story told to the people of Makkah, so they could see where the path they had picked was heading.
now: You go along with the group joke about the new kid, the office shortcut, the friend's plan you know is wrong. {trap}Going along is still going.{/trap} {idea}You can step off at any point before the end.{/idea}
old: I am not responsible if I only followed others.
new: Following someone means sharing their road; choosing whom I follow is my responsibility.
try: Notice one thing you do only because others do it, and decide for yourself whether to keep doing it.

title: Seven gates, each one matched to deeds.
subtitle: Nothing about it is random
then: Ibn Kathir explains that for each gate a portion of the followers of Iblis is decreed, and {idea}each one will enter a gate according to his deeds, and settle in a level according to his deeds{/idea}. He adds, {trap}may Allah save us from that{/trap}.
now: You tell yourself your sins are small compared to others, or so big nothing matters anymore. {idea}Both are wrong. Every deed is weighed exactly.{/idea} That means every good deed you add today also counts.
old: My sins are either too small to matter or too big to fix.
new: Allah measures every deed exactly, so each wrong avoided and each good done truly counts.
try: Make the dua Ibn Kathir made: O Allah, save me from the Fire. Then do one good deed.
